big: Dadi's neighbour bought a plan that promised 'insurance plus savings plus guaranteed returns'. After four years she needed to stop paying. She got back far less than she had put in.

lines: The agent said I get cover and my money back with profit. Why would anyone buy a plain term plan then?
Because the extras always come at a cost. Let us look at what is inside these plans, and what stopping early costs.

title: Savings-linked plans
stops: Stopping early can return much less than you paid
An insurance policy promises investment returns
A ULIP deducts charges from premium and fund
Every policy is a good fit for every buyer
caps: If you stop early, the surrender value is often far below the premiums paid.
Insurance is protection. Promising investment returns from it is mis-selling.
A ULIP mixes cover and investment, and charges are deducted along the way.
Match the product to the purpose. Do not buy savings through cover.

rows: Life cover plus savings, pays a maturity amount if you survive
Cover plus market-linked investment, with charges
What you get if you stop before the term ends
note: A common approach is a plain term plan for cover and a separate investment for growth, so each does one job well.

q: Dadi stops an endowment plan after four years. What is the likely result?
opts: She often gets much less than she paid, called the surrender value
She gets back all premiums with interest
She gets the full maturity amount, since she paid for four years
She gets a bonus for starting the plan early
why: Surrender value is often far lower than premiums paid, especially in early years.
Stopping early usually does not return all premiums, and interest is not assured.
The maturity amount is paid only if the term is completed.
Stopping early does not earn a bonus. It often costs the saver.

q: An agent tells Rohan an insurance policy will give 'guaranteed 12% returns'. What should Rohan do?
opts: Accept it, since insurers are all regulated bodies in India
Buy two such policies at once, to stay on the safe side
Be careful, since promised returns may be mis-selling
Pay in cash, so that nobody is able to check the deal
why: Regulation does not make every claim by an agent true, so he should read the policy.
Buying more of a doubtful product multiplies the problem instead of solving it.
Exaggerated claims and hidden costs are mis-selling, so he should read the terms and question it.
Paying in cash removes the paper trail and does not help him in any way.

q: What do the charges inside a ULIP do?
opts: Nothing, since the insurer pays them from its own pocket
Reduce the money invested, so returns lag the fund's growth
Raise the sum assured at the end of the whole term
Pay only for the agent's yearly holiday and nothing else
why: Charges are taken from the policyholder's premium and fund, not paid by the insurer.
Costs are deducted along the way, so what grows is smaller than the fund's headline gain.
Charges do not raise the sum assured. They reduce what is invested.
Charges cover costs and commissions in general, not one single item.

q: Meena wants cover and growth. Which approach keeps each job separate?
opts: One endowment plan that does both jobs at once
A ULIP, since it covers both jobs in one place
Skip the cover and invest the whole amount instead
A plain term plan plus a separate investment
why: A combined plan mixes two goals, and it can do both less well than separate tools.
A ULIP also mixes the two, with charges deducted from the premium and fund.
Skipping cover leaves the family exposed if the earner is gone, so it is a poor choice.
A term plan covers the risk at low cost, and a separate investment can suit her goal.

pts: Stopping a savings plan early often returns much less than you paid.
Insurance is protection. Promising investment returns from it is a warning sign.
Keep cover and investing separate: term plan plus a separate investment.
